glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 6 warns a son against traps that catch a careless life, a rash pledge, lazy sleep, and the lying, discord-sowing ways the LORD hates, and then holds up his parents’ commandment as a lamp that keeps him from the fire of adultery.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The chapter stands between the warning against the immoral woman in chapter 5 and the full scene of chapter 7. Four short warnings come first (6:1–19), and then the father’s “My son” at 6:20 leads back to adultery.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Can a man take fire to his bosom, And his clothes not be burned?” (Proverbs 6:27)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 6 pauses in the father’s warnings about adultery to name other traps, and each begins small. A son shakes hands on a friend’s debt and is “snared by the words of your mouth” (6:2). A sluggard asks for “A little sleep, a little slumber” (6:10), and poverty arrives “like a prowler” (6:11). Wisdom, the skill of living life God’s way, is shown here in what a man promises and how he works. The ant has no overseer, yet she gathers her food in harvest, and the sluggard is told, “Consider her ways and be wise” (6:6).

The chapter then turns to wickedness and shows what God thinks of it. The worthless man winks, shuffles, points, and “sows discord” (6:14). Next comes the list of what “the LORD hates” (6:16), which opens with “A proud look” and saves for last “one who sows discord among brethren” (6:17, 19). His hatred of these things comes from His goodness, because each one wounds people He loves.

When “My son” returns, the father answers temptation with teaching bound on the heart, a lamp for every hour. His question, “Can a man take fire to his bosom, And his clothes not be burned?” (6:27), tells the son that adultery cannot be handled safely, because the man who commits it “destroys his own soul” (6:32).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 6:1–5 — Get Free from a Rash Pledge

A son who has guaranteed a neighbor’s debt has been caught by his own quick words, so the father tells him to set his pride aside and plead for release before he lets himself sleep. The counsel guards against careless pledges without forbidding generosity, which the book commends elsewhere (11:24–25).

Proverbs 6:6–11 — Go to the Ant, You Sluggard

The sluggard is sent to learn from the ant, which works with no one standing over her and gathers food while the season allows. His own drowsy excuses show how small delays add up until need overtakes him like an armed man.

Proverbs 6:12–15 — The Worthless Troublemaker

The worthless man deceives with his whole person, through a twisted mouth, a wink, a shuffle of the feet, and a pointing finger, because his heart keeps plotting evil and planting strife. The ruin he works on others comes back on him suddenly and cannot be repaired.

Proverbs 6:16–19 — Seven Things the LORD Hates

A counting pattern builds to seven things the LORD finds detestable, beginning with a proud look and tracing sin through the eyes, tongue, hands, heart, and feet. The list ends with the one who sows discord among brethren, the same sin that marked the troublemaker just before it.

Proverbs 6:20–23 — The Commandment Is a Lamp

The father calls his son back to both parents’ teaching and tells him to bind it on his heart, where it will guide him as he walks, guard him as he sleeps, and speak with him when he wakes. Even their correction lights the way of life.

Proverbs 6:24–35 — Fire in the Bosom

That light keeps the son from the seductress, and the warning starts with desire in the heart and the pull of her eyes, before any act. Questions about fire and hot coals, and a comparison with a hungry thief, show that adultery costs a man his own soul and stirs a husband’s anger that no gift can quiet.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 6 brings wisdom down to the details of an ordinary week: a signature on someone else’s debt, a morning slept away, a wink across the room. The father treats these as real dangers because small, repeated choices decide where a life ends up. His portrait is of a man who will not work, never of one who cannot; illness, disability, and genuine need lie outside this warning.

The chapter also shows how much God cares about the peace of His people. Sowing discord stands beside lying and the shedding of innocent blood among the things He hates, and Jesus later blesses the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9). The warning about adultery locates the battle in the heart (6:25; compare Matthew 5:28). Its reproach among people lasts (6:33), yet Proverbs also promises that “whoever confesses and forsakes them will have mercy” (28:13).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Traps that start small. A quick handshake, a little more sleep, and a lingering look each lead to losses far larger than the first step (6:1–2, 10–11, 25–26).

Urgency to get free. The son is to give his eyes no sleep until he is released from the pledge, escaping like a gazelle from the hunter or a bird from the fowler (6:3–5).

Sin in the whole person. Mouth, eyes, feet, fingers, hands, and heart all appear in the troublemaker and in the list of what the LORD hates, because sin starts inside and comes out through the body (6:12–14, 17–18).

Discord among brethren. Sowing discord marks the worthless man and closes the LORD’s list, showing how seriously God takes the breaking of peace (6:14, 19).

Teaching kept in the heart. Parents’ commands bound on the heart lead, keep, and counsel the son, and they are what guard him from the seductress (6:20–24).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Surety (6:1). A person who guarantees someone else’s debt, much like cosigning a loan today. A handshake sealed the pledge, and the one who gave it became liable if the borrower failed.

Sluggard (6:6, 9). The NKJV uses this word only here; elsewhere Proverbs speaks of the lazy man. He lacks self-discipline and keeps putting off what must be done, which the ant’s steady work exposes.

A worthless person (6:12). A wicked man who uses his mouth, gestures, and heart to stir up trouble. His winks and signals are the outward show of a scheming heart.

Abomination (6:16). Something the LORD finds detestable. The pattern of six and then seven builds toward the last item for emphasis and does not set six against seven.

Fire in the bosom (6:27). The bosom is the fold of a garment at the chest. Carrying fire there means certain harm, the father’s picture of what adultery does to the man who commits it.

Restore sevenfold (6:31). Most likely full repayment rather than a fixed legal amount. The thief may lose everything in his house, yet his debt can be paid, while the wronged husband “will accept no recompense” (6:35).

focus: Proverbs 6 gathers practical warnings about rash pledges, laziness, the worthless troublemaker, and the seven things the LORD hates, and then returns to the commandment as a lamp that guards the son from adultery.

sections.title: Get Free from a Rash Pledge
sections.summary: If the son has become surety for a neighbor, he is to go and humble himself without delay to deliver himself, like a gazelle from the hunter.

sections.title: Go to the Ant, You Sluggard
sections.summary: The sluggard is to learn from the ant, which gathers its food in harvest without a ruler. A little sleep and folding of the hands will bring poverty like a prowler.

sections.title: The Worthless Troublemaker
sections.summary: The worthless person walks with a perverse mouth and devious gestures, devises evil, and sows discord, and calamity will come on him suddenly.

sections.title: Seven Things the LORD Hates
sections.summary: Six things the LORD hates, and seven are an abomination to Him, from a proud look and a lying tongue to one who sows discord among brethren.

sections.title: The Commandment Is a Lamp
sections.summary: The son is to bind his parents’ commands on his heart, for they will lead and keep him. The commandment is a lamp, the law a light, and reproofs of instruction the way of life.

sections.title: Fire in the Bosom
sections.summary: That teaching will keep him from the seductress whose beauty he must not desire. As no one can carry fire in his bosom without being burned, whoever goes in to a neighbor’s wife will not go unpunished, and the husband’s jealousy will accept no ransom.

1.brief: The father raises a practical danger: becoming surety, guaranteeing a friend’s debt or shaking hands on a pledge for a stranger. A quick promise to cover someone else’s obligation can tie a person to a debt he does not control.
1.explain:
“My son, if you become surety for your friend,”

The father turns to a new danger, one that has to do with money and promises. To become “surety” was to guarantee another person’s debt: if the borrower failed to pay, the one who had pledged became liable for it. The nearest modern equivalent is cosigning a loan. “Your friend” translates the ordinary Hebrew word for a neighbor or companion, someone the son knows. That is part of the danger. A rash pledge usually begins with goodwill: a friend is in need, a lender wants security, and the son steps in with his name.

“If you have shaken hands in pledge for a stranger,”

In Israel an agreement of this kind was sealed by striking hands, a public gesture that bound a man to his word, and Proverbs returns to the practice more than once (17:18; 22:26). The “stranger” is someone outside the son’s circle, whether the lender to whom he is now bound or another party whose debts he has agreed to carry. Either way, he has tied his future to the faithfulness of someone he cannot control. Proverbs commends generosity elsewhere: “He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD” (19:17). The father is not forbidding help. He is warning against a hasty guarantee that hands one’s security to another person’s choices. Wisdom gives freely what it can afford to lose and avoids promises it may not be able to keep.
1.notes:
Whether the “friend” and the “stranger” of 6:1 are the same person, or the friend is the borrower and the stranger the creditor, is debated. The ESV and NASB render “friend” as “neighbor,” which shows the general sense of the Hebrew word.

“Shaken hands” renders a Hebrew phrase that means to strike the palms, the gesture that sealed the pledge. The KJV keeps the picture of a hand “stricken” with a stranger.

2.brief: By that pledge the son is snared and caught by the words of his own mouth. The repeated line stresses that his own promise, spoken too quickly, has become the trap that holds him.
2.explain:
“You are snared by the words of your mouth;”

The trap was not set by an enemy. The son is snared by his own words. A promise spoken in a moment of sympathy, pressure or pride has become a snare that holds him. The father wants his son to see that words create obligations. What comes out of his mouth can bind his hands and his future for years.

“You are taken by the words of your mouth.”

The second line repeats the first almost exactly, changing only the verb. “Taken” means captured, caught like an animal in a trap or a city in war. The repetition presses the point home: it was his own mouth. A single pledge has put him in the power of others. The father does not tell him to treat his word as if it meant nothing. Because his word is real and binding, he must now take honorable steps to be released from it.

3.brief: The remedy is urgent and humbling: “So do this, my son, and deliver yourself,” for he is now in his friend’s power. He must go, swallow his pride, and press his friend to release him from the pledge.
3.explain:
“So do this, my son, and deliver yourself;”

The father moves from diagnosis to remedy, and his tone becomes urgent. To “deliver yourself” is to rescue yourself and get free. He does not tell the son to quietly break his word or to wait and hope that the borrower pays. He tells him to act.

“For you have come into the hand of your friend:”

“Into the hand of” means into someone’s power. By pledging, the son has placed his security under another person’s control. Whether this friend is the borrower whose debt he guaranteed or the one who now holds his pledge, the son is no longer free to manage his own affairs.

“Go and humble yourself;”

The way out requires humility. The son must set aside his pride, admit that he promised too quickly, and seek release. Pride would rather stay trapped than confess a mistake, and many people remain in difficulties they could have left because they would not humble themselves and ask.

“Plead with your friend.”

To “plead” here is to press hard, to ask persistently and refuse to accept a casual no. The father does not counsel a polite inquiry. He counsels earnest, repeated appeal until the son is released from the obligation. The energy that was missing when the promise was made must now go into getting free of it.
3.notes: The two Hebrew verbs behind “humble yourself” and “plead” are rare. The first appears elsewhere only in Psalm 68:30, and its basic sense is to stamp or trample, which here suggests a man lowering himself before another. The second means to press or urge hard. Translations therefore vary: the NKJV and NASB read “humble yourself,” the ESV has “hasten” and “plead urgently,” and the NASB “importune.” All of them stress humble, persistent pressing.

4.brief: He is not to give sleep to his eyes or rest to his eyelids until the matter is settled. Delay only tightens the trap, so getting free must come before comfort.
4.explain:
“Give no sleep to your eyes,”

The urgency becomes concrete. The son is not to go to bed with the matter unsettled. A debt guaranteed for someone else can grow, and a creditor’s patience can run out. Every night of delay tightens the trap, so getting free must come before comfort.

“Nor slumber to your eyelids.”

The second line repeats the first for emphasis: rest must wait until he is free. The same pair of Hebrew words, translated sleep and slumber, returns a few lines later in the sluggard’s request for “A little sleep, a little slumber” (6:10). The son caught by a rash pledge must give up sleep for a time; the sluggard who gives himself to sleep loses everything. Sleep is good in its place, and wisdom knows when it must wait.

5.brief: The son must free himself like a gazelle escaping the hunter’s hand or a bird escaping the fowler. The images picture a desperate, all-out effort to get loose, the opposite of the careless way he got caught.
5.explain:
“Deliver yourself like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter,”

A gazelle caught by a hunter does not relax or wait to see what will happen. It struggles with all its strength to get loose. The gazelle was proverbial for speed; Scripture says of one fast runner that he “was as fleet of foot as a wild gazelle” (2 Samuel 2:18). The father wants the same quick, all-out effort from his son.

“And like a bird from the hand of the fowler.”

A fowler was a bird-catcher who used nets and snares. A bird caught in his trap beats its wings until it escapes. The two pictures together describe a creature that knows it is caught and will not rest until it is free. The careless way the son got into the trap, with a handshake and a few words, stands in sharp contrast to the desperate effort needed to get out. A psalm uses the same picture for rescue: “Our soul has escaped as a bird from the snare of the fowlers” (Psalm 124:7).

6.brief: The father sends the sluggard to a tiny teacher: “Go to the ant, you sluggard!” The lazy man is told to study the ant’s ways and become wise, for even an insect can shame the one who will not work.
6.explain:
“Go to the ant, you sluggard!”

The father turns to a new figure, the sluggard. The NKJV uses this word only here and in 6:9; elsewhere Proverbs speaks of the lazy man. The sluggard is not someone who cannot work because of illness, disability or genuine hardship. He is someone who will not work. He lacks self-discipline, keeps putting off what must be done, and loves his sleep. The father sends him to school, and the teacher is an ant. There is gentle mockery in the command: a man made in God’s image is told to go and learn from one of the smallest creatures he could step on.

“Consider her ways and be wise,”

To “consider” is to look carefully and study. The ant’s “ways” are her habits of life. The goal is that the sluggard will “be wise,” gaining the skill for living that he lacks. Wisdom in Proverbs is practical, and here it means the skill of working steadily and preparing ahead. God has built lessons into His creation, and the humble can learn from them. Work itself belonged to God’s good design before sin entered the world, for the LORD put the man in the garden “to tend and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). The sluggard’s laziness quietly refuses that design.
6.notes: “Sluggard” appears in the NKJV of Proverbs only at 6:6 and 6:9; the same Hebrew word is rendered “lazy man” elsewhere in the book (for example 13:4 and 26:13–16).

7.brief: What makes the ant remarkable is that she has no captain, overseer, or ruler driving her. She works without anyone watching or commanding, which is the self-discipline the sluggard lacks.
7.explain:
“Which, having no captain, Overseer or ruler,”

The ant’s remarkable trait is that she works without a boss. “Captain,” “Overseer” and “ruler” are three titles of authority: a chief who commands, an officer who supervises and a ruler who governs. The ant has none of them standing over her, and still she works. The sluggard needs to be pushed, reminded and driven, and even then he does little. The ant needs no one to watch her. This is self-discipline: doing what needs to be done because it needs to be done, without waiting for someone to enforce it. The lesson does not condemn leaders or supervision. It exposes the person who works only when he is watched.

8.brief: Still she gathers her supplies in summer and her food at harvest, working while the time allows. The ant prepares ahead of time, while the sluggard lets the opportunity pass.
8.explain:
“Provides her supplies in the summer,”

Summer is the season of warmth and growth, when food is available. The ant uses it. She gathers while there is something to gather, before the season changes and food is scarce.

“And gathers her food in the harvest.”

The harvest is the time of gathering crops, a window that does not stay open long. The ant works ahead of her need and stores what she will eat later. The lesson is foresight: wisdom recognizes the season and uses it. The sluggard lets the opportunity pass and finds himself without supply after the season has turned. Some opportunities come only once a year, and some only once in a lifetime; the ant does not waste hers.

9.brief: Two questions confront the sluggard: “How long will you slumber, O sluggard?” and when will he rise from his sleep? The father addresses him directly, exposing a habit of putting off what must be done.
9.explain:
“How long will you slumber, O sluggard?”

The father now speaks to the sluggard directly. “How long” implies that the sleeping has already gone on far too long. The question is a rebuke, but it also calls him to get up, and it assumes that he still can.

“When will you rise from your sleep?”

The second question presses further. “When” asks for a time, and the sluggard never has one. He always intends to rise later. These questions expose the habit of putting things off. The sluggard rarely refuses to work outright; he simply never finds the right moment to begin, and the moment he is waiting for never comes.

10.brief: The sluggard’s reply is pictured in his own drowsy words: a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands. Each delay seems small and harmless, but together they become a way of life.
10.explain:
“A little sleep, a little slumber,”

The father now voices the sluggard’s own reply. Each request is small: just a little more sleep, just a little more rest. No single delay seems harmful, and that is the trap. The repeated “a little” shows how the sluggard thinks. He never asks for a ruined life. He only asks for a few more minutes, again and again.

“A little folding of the hands to sleep—”

Folded hands are hands at rest, doing nothing, the opposite of the ant’s busy work. The dash at the end of the NKJV line shows that the thought runs straight into 6:11, where all these little delays add up to something large. A way of life is built from small choices repeated, and the sluggard’s life is built from many small postponements.
10.notes: 6:10–11 return almost word for word in 24:33–34, as the lesson drawn from the overgrown field of the lazy man (24:30–34). The NKJV reads “to sleep” in 6:10 and “to rest” in 24:33.

11.brief: The result is poverty that comes on him like a prowler and need like an armed man. Ruin arrives suddenly and overpowers him, though it has been building quietly through every small delay.
11.explain:
“So shall your poverty come on you like a prowler,”

The consequence arrives. Poverty comes like a prowler, someone who moves about quietly and arrives unexpectedly. The sluggard does not see poverty approaching. It slips up on him while he sleeps. Each small delay seemed harmless, but together they have opened the door.

“And your need like an armed man.”

“Need” is want, the lack of what is necessary. It comes like an armed man, someone who cannot be resisted. When poverty finally arrives, the sluggard has no defense against it. The two pictures move from stealth to force: consequences gather quietly and then overwhelm. This describes where persistent idleness usually leads. Proverbs does not teach that all poverty comes from laziness, and nothing here permits the reader to blame the sick, the disabled or the needy for their circumstances. The father is warning a capable son about his own habits.
11.notes: “Prowler” renders a Hebrew expression for one who walks about or travels, and the KJV keeps that sense: ‘one that travelleth.’ Other versions bring out the threat: the NASB has “vagabond,” the ESV “robber,” and the current NIV “thief.” “Armed man” is literally, in Hebrew, ‘a man of the shield,’ a soldier equipped for battle.

12.brief: A new figure appears: the worthless person, a wicked man who goes about with a perverse mouth. His twisted speech is the first mark of a life given over to trouble.
12.explain:
“A worthless person, a wicked man,”

The father turns to another figure, and this one is worse than the sluggard. The sluggard harms himself by doing nothing; this man harms others by what he does. “A worthless person” translates a Hebrew expression for a man of no value and real wickedness, someone destructive as well as useless. “A wicked man” adds that his whole life is set against what is right.

“Walks with a perverse mouth;”

To “walk” is to live, to go about one’s life. His speech is “perverse,” twisted and crooked, the opposite of honest and straight. Deceitful talk is not an occasional slip for him; it is the way he goes through life. The father describes him from the outside in, beginning with the mouth, moving through his body, and reaching his heart in 6:14. Wisdom learns to recognize such a person before being drawn into his schemes.
12.notes: “A worthless person” is literally, in Hebrew, ‘a man of belial.’ Here belial is not a personal name but the Hebrew word for worthlessness, describing someone good for nothing and destructive. The KJV and other older versions left the word untranslated, which is why it can sound like a name. The same word describes Eli’s sons in 1 Samuel 2:12, where the KJV has ‘sons of Belial’ and the NKJV renders it “corrupt.”

13.brief: He also speaks with his body, winking, shuffling his feet, and pointing with his fingers. These secret signals show a man who deceives and schemes even when he says nothing aloud.
13.explain:
“He winks with his eyes,”

The troublemaker communicates without words. A wink is a secret signal, a way of letting an accomplice know that what is being said is not what is meant, or of mocking someone behind his back.

“He shuffles his feet,”

Movements of the feet serve as further signals. Like the wink, they send hidden messages, perhaps to coordinate with others or to mislead the person being deceived.

“He points with his fingers;”

Pointing fingers can direct attention, accuse, or signal to a partner. Together, eyes, feet and fingers show a man whose whole body serves his deceit. His mouth says one thing while his body says another. Winking and gesturing are not wrong in themselves. A deceitful heart simply puts every part of the person to work for its schemes. The signals may fool the people around him, but they do not hide anything from God.
13.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “shuffles his feet” is usually understood as scraping or rubbing the feet, a movement used to make secret signs; some scholars instead connect it with a verb meaning to speak. The KJV’s “speaketh” expresses that signalling sense, and the ESV and NASB read “signals.”

14.brief: Perversity fills his heart, he keeps plotting evil, and he sows discord among others. His mouth and gestures flow from a corrupt heart, and the harvest he plants is strife.
14.explain:
“Perversity is in his heart,”

Now the source appears. His twisted mouth and secret signals flow from a heart full of perversity, a deliberate crookedness that turns what is straight. Proverbs treats the heart as the inner person, the place of thought, will and desire, and teaches that the whole course of a life comes from it: “Keep your heart with all diligence, For out of it spring the issues of life” (4:23).

“He devises evil continually,”

To “devise” is to plot and plan. He does not stumble into evil; he thinks it up on purpose. “Continually” shows that this is his steady occupation. His mind is always at work on some new harm.

“He sows discord.”

“Discord” is strife and quarreling between people. To “sow” it is to plant it on purpose and let it grow, as a farmer scatters seed. The troublemaker spreads conflict among people who would otherwise live in peace. His rumors, half-truths and whispered suggestions do their work long after he has moved on. The phrase links his portrait directly to the list that follows, which ends with “one who sows discord among brethren” (6:19).

15.brief: Therefore calamity will come on him suddenly, and he will be broken beyond remedy. The one who caused others to fall will himself be shattered without warning or repair.
15.explain:
“Therefore his calamity shall come suddenly;”

“Therefore” ties his end to his way of life. He devised evil “continually,” but his ruin comes “suddenly.” The man who spent his life arranging trouble for others does not see his own trouble coming. Calamity arrives without warning.

“Suddenly he shall be broken without remedy.”

The word “Suddenly” is repeated for emphasis. “Broken” means shattered, as a clay pot is smashed. “Without remedy” means there is no healing and no repair. The schemer who broke the peace of others is himself broken beyond mending. The verse does not say when this will happen, and it may be long delayed, but the end is certain. A wicked man may seem untouchable for years. God’s justice can wait and then arrive in a moment, and delay is no guarantee of safety.
15.notes: In Hebrew “without remedy” reads literally ‘and there is no healing.’ The noun for healing is the same word rendered “health” where the father says his words are “health to all their flesh” (4:22). The schemer is left without the healing that wisdom gives.

16.brief: The father introduces a list with a counting pattern: six things the LORD hates, and seven that are an abomination to Him. The form builds toward the seventh item for emphasis, showing what God finds detestable.
16.explain:
“These six things the LORD hates,”

The father now speaks of what the LORD Himself hates. The word is strong, and it is meant to be. God is not neutral toward evil that destroys people. His hatred of these things comes from His goodness and holiness: He hates what wounds the people He loves and what contradicts His own character. The list describes ways of acting, and every item on it is something a person can turn from.

“Yes, seven are an abomination to Him:”

The pattern of six and then seven is a Hebrew way of building a list toward a climax. Agur uses the same form: “There are three things which are too wonderful for me, Yes, four which I do not understand” (30:18). The form does not mean that the first six are hated less, and nothing should be built on the difference between six and seven. It gives the final item special emphasis. An “abomination” is something God finds detestable, utterly offensive to Him. In Proverbs the word often stands opposite what is “His delight” (11:20). The list moves through the body, eyes, tongue, hands, heart and feet, and ends with the sin that destroys community.
16.notes: The same rising-number pattern appears in the prophets, “For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four” (Amos 1:3), and repeatedly in 30:15–31.

17.brief: The first three are a proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood. The list begins with pride, then moves through the body from the eyes to the tongue to the hands, from arrogance to deceit to violence.
17.explain:
“A proud look,”

The list begins with pride. “A proud look” describes eyes lifted up in arrogance, looking down on others. Pride heads the list because so much else grows from it; the one who thinks himself above others and above correction is ready to lie, harm and divide. Wisdom says the same in chapter 8: “Pride and arrogance and the evil way And the perverse mouth I hate” (8:13).

“A lying tongue,”

The second item is deceitful speech. A lying tongue says what is false to gain an advantage or avoid exposure. The worthless man of 6:12 walked with a perverse mouth, and here God names lying as something He hates. God is truthful, and lies attack the trust that every relationship depends on.

“Hands that shed innocent blood,”

The third item is violence against the innocent: killing or harming someone who has done nothing to deserve it. The list moves from arrogance in the eyes to deceit on the tongue to violence in the hands, showing how sin spreads through a person and grows worse as it goes. Scripture treats the shedding of innocent blood with the utmost seriousness, because every human being bears God’s image: “For in the image of God He made man” (Genesis 9:6).
17.notes: In Hebrew “a proud look” is literally ‘eyes raised high.’ The ESV and NASB render it “haughty eyes,” and the KJV margin gives the same literal sense: ‘Heb. Haughty eyes.’

18.brief: Next come a heart that devises wicked plans and feet quick to run to evil. Sin is traced from the inward plotting of the heart to the eager feet that carry it out.
18.explain:
“A heart that devises wicked plans,”

The fourth item moves inward to the source. A heart that devises wicked plans is one that schemes, working out harm before it acts. The same Hebrew verb described the troublemaker who “devises evil continually” (6:14). God sees the planning behind the act as well as the act itself.

“Feet that are swift in running to evil,”

The fifth item describes eagerness for wrong. These feet do not stumble into evil reluctantly; they run to it. The order is telling. The heart plans, and the feet carry out the plan in a hurry. Chapter 1 described the violent gang in the same terms: “For their feet run to evil” (1:16). The father’s warnings are meant to slow his son’s feet before they ever learn that pace.

19.brief: The list ends with a false witness who speaks lies and one who sows discord among brethren. The seventh and climactic item is the very sin of the troublemaker just described, showing how seriously God takes the breaking of peace among His people.
19.explain:
“A false witness who speaks lies,”

The sixth item is lying in a formal setting. A false witness testifies falsely in court or in a public dispute, and his lies can cost an innocent person his reputation, property or life. The commandment had forbidden it: “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:16). A lying tongue (6:17) covered falsehood in general; here falsehood becomes a weapon in the very place where justice should be done.

“And one who sows discord among brethren.”

The seventh item, in the place of emphasis, is the person who stirs up strife among brothers, among people who belong together. The phrase repeats the troublemaker’s sin from 6:14. The list began with pride and ends with broken brotherhood, as though tracing where arrogance finally leads. “Brethren” points to family and to the community of God’s people, who are meant to live in unity. By placing this sin last, the list shows how seriously God takes the breaking of peace among His people.
19.notes: Five of the seven items echo the portrait of 6:12–15: the eyes (6:13, 17), the mouth and tongue (6:12, 17), the feet (6:13, 18), the heart that devises evil (6:14, 18) and the sowing of discord, which ends both units (6:14, 19). The order is not identical, but the second unit gives God’s verdict on the kind of man described in the first.

20.brief: The father returns to his central appeal: “My son, keep your father’s command,” and do not forsake your mother’s law. Once again both parents’ teaching stands together as the son’s guide.
20.explain:
“My son, keep your father’s command,”

The father returns to the address that opened the chapter and to his central appeal. To “keep” is to guard and obey, to hold on to something valuable. “Command” is the father’s teaching given with authority. In a faithful home that teaching carries God’s ways from one generation to the next. With 6:20 the last unit of the chapter begins, and it leads into a renewed warning against adultery.

“And do not forsake the law of your mother.”

The mother’s teaching stands beside the father’s, as it did when the father first spoke in chapter 1: “do not forsake the law of your mother” (1:8). “Law” here means instruction, the guidance a mother gives her children. Both parents’ teaching together guides the son. To “forsake” is to abandon or leave behind, and the danger is often a slow drift away from what was taught at home more than a single open rebellion.
20.notes: The verse closely echoes 1:8. There the son is to “hear the instruction of your father”; here he is to “keep your father’s command.” The second line is the same in both verses.

21.brief: The son is to bind these commands continually on his heart and tie them around his neck. Parental instruction is to be kept close and constant, part of his inner life and visible in his conduct.
21.explain:
“Bind them continually upon your heart;”

The son is to keep his parents’ teaching close and constant. “Bind” pictures tying something securely so it cannot be lost. “Upon your heart” means at the center of his inner life, where thoughts, desires and decisions arise. “Continually” means at all times, not only when it is convenient. Teaching held this way is ready when it is needed most.

“Tie them around your neck.”

Something tied around the neck is visible and always present, like a necklace. The parents’ teaching is to mark how the son lives in public as well as what he thinks in private. The language echoes 3:3, “Bind them around your neck, Write them on the tablet of your heart.” It also recalls Moses’ charge to Israel to bind God’s words “as a sign on your hand” (Deuteronomy 6:8), which places the parents’ teaching within the larger work of passing God’s ways to the next generation.

22.brief: This teaching will lead him when he walks, guard him when he sleeps, and speak to him when he wakes. The word kept in the heart becomes a companion for every hour, guiding, protecting, and counseling.
22.explain:
“When you roam, they will lead you;”

Now the father describes what this teaching does. “When you roam” means whenever you go about your daily life. The teaching will lead him, guiding his steps like a companion who knows the way.

“When you sleep, they will keep you;”

Even in sleep, when he is least alert, the teaching will keep him, guarding and protecting him. Instruction stored in the heart goes on working when the mind is at rest. The line brings comfort into a chapter that has twice spoken of sleep: the son who must not sleep until he is free of his pledge (6:4) and the sluggard who sleeps too much (6:9–10). Here sleep is under protection.

“And when you awake, they will speak with you.”

When he wakes, the teaching will be there to speak with him, to counsel him and set his mind on the right way at the start of the day. The three lines cover the whole day, walking, sleeping and waking, much as Moses told Israel to talk of God’s words “when you walk by the way, when you lie down, and when you rise up” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Teaching received in this way becomes a voice the son carries with him everywhere.

23.brief: The commandment is a lamp, the law a light, and the reproofs of instruction are the way of life. Even correction, though it stings, lights the path toward life rather than standing in the way of it.
23.explain:
“For the commandment is a lamp,”

“For” explains why the teaching can lead, keep and speak. The commandment is a lamp, a small light carried in the hand. Ancient lamps did not light up a whole landscape; they showed the next step on the path in the dark.

“And the law a light;”

“The law” is the same instruction named in 6:20, and it gives light that shows the way. The pairing of lamp and light stresses that God’s ways, faithfully taught, make the path visible. A psalm uses the same pairing for God’s word: “Your word is a lamp to my feet And a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). The darkness the father has in mind is about to be named, for the next lines turn to the seductress, whose work is done at night.

“Reproofs of instruction are the way of life,”

“Reproofs” are corrections, words that tell a person he is wrong. The father calls them “the way of life,” the road that leads to life. Correction stings, but it belongs to the path; it is not a detour from it. The ruined man of chapter 5 hated correction and came to the edge of total ruin in 5:12–14. The son who accepts reproof walks the way of life. The comma at the end of the line shows that the sentence continues into 6:24, where the purpose of this lamp is named.

24.brief: One purpose of this lamp is to keep the son from the evil woman and the flattering tongue of a seductress. The same instruction that lights his path protects him from the smooth words that would lead him astray.
24.explain:
“To keep you from the evil woman,”

One purpose of the lamp is protection. The teaching that leads and keeps the son will keep him from the evil woman. “Evil” describes her conduct. She is the adulterous woman of chapters 2, 5 and 7, a married woman who betrays her husband, as the mention of a “neighbor’s wife” and a jealous husband in 6:29 and 6:34 makes clear. The warning concerns her chosen path and the son’s response to it; it is not a warning about women in general.

“From the flattering tongue of a seductress.”

As in 2:16 and 5:3, her weapon is speech. A “flattering” tongue is smooth, pleasant and easy to believe. “Seductress” again marks her as an outsider to the son’s home and to God’s ways; the text does not settle her nationality. The son needs a lamp because flattery works best in the dark, where no light shows where its words lead. The father’s teaching gives him a truer voice to listen to than hers.
24.notes: The Hebrew wording behind “the evil woman” is unusual, and translators have long discussed it. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, reads “married woman” here, and some modern versions, the NRSV among them, follow the Greek at this point. The NKJV follows the standard Hebrew reading at this point.

25.brief: He must not desire her beauty in his heart or let her capture him with her eyelids. The battle begins inwardly, in desire and in the glance, long before any act is committed.
25.explain:
“Do not lust after her beauty in your heart,”

The father locates the battle where it begins, in the heart. The Hebrew verb behind “lust after” means to desire and covet, to want what belongs to another. Noticing beauty is not the sin. The command concerns letting desire for her take root and grow. Long before any act, the heart decides what it will want. Jesus later drew out the same truth, that adultery can be committed “in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). Her beauty is not condemned, and she is not blamed for having it; the son is warned about his own desire.

“Nor let her allure you with her eyelids.”

“Eyelids” pictures her glances, the look meant to attract and invite. The Hebrew verb behind “allure” is the ordinary word for taking, and here it means to capture. A glance welcomed into the heart becomes a snare. The father wants his son to guard his eyes as well as his heart, because the eyes are so often the door through which desire enters. The two lines together show both sides of temptation: the son’s own desire and her deliberate attraction.
25.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “lust after” is the same verb used in the commandment “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exodus 20:17), so the father’s warning uses the very language of the Tenth Commandment.

26.brief: A harlot can reduce a man to a crust of bread, and an adulteress hunts for his very life. The cost of sexual sin moves from losing money to losing one’s precious life.
26.explain:
“For by means of a harlot”

“For” introduces the reason for the warning. A harlot is a prostitute, a woman who sells sexual favors. The father begins with her and then moves to the adulteress, comparing what each one costs.

“A man is reduced to a crust of bread;”

Going to a prostitute can bring a man down to poverty, to his last piece of bread. The Hebrew of this line is compact and can be read in more than one way, but the NKJV’s sense is clear: sexual sin of this kind drains a man’s resources until he has almost nothing left.

“And an adulteress will prey upon his precious life.”

The adulteress, a woman married to another man, is more dangerous still. She does not merely cost money; she will prey upon his precious life. The Hebrew verb here pictures a hunter stalking game. What is at stake now is the man’s very life, which God regards as precious. As costly as prostitution is, adultery with another man’s wife puts everything at risk, because it brings down the fury of a wronged husband (6:34–35) and destroys the man’s own soul (6:32).
26.notes:
The first two lines are read differently in the versions. The NKJV, the NASB and the 1984 edition of the NIV take them as a man being brought down to a loaf or crust of bread. The ESV and the current NIV (2011) read them as a statement about price (ESV: ‘the price of a prostitute is only a loaf of bread’). On either reading the line sets a lesser cost beside the deadly cost of adultery.

In Hebrew “adulteress” is literally ‘a man’s wife,’ that is, a woman married to another man, as the KJV margin notes (‘the woman of a man, or, a man’s wife’).

27.brief: The father asks, “Can a man take fire to his bosom, And his clothes not be burned?” The obvious answer exposes the folly of thinking anyone can play with adultery and escape harm.
27.explain:
“Can a man take fire to his bosom,”

The father asks a question with an obvious answer. The “bosom” is the chest, or the fold of a garment at the chest where a person might carry something close. No one can carry fire there safely; fire held against the body will burn.

“And his clothes not be burned?”

Of course his clothes will burn. The question exposes the folly of thinking a man can play with adultery and escape harm. Sexual desire is God’s good gift within marriage, as 5:15–19 celebrates. Outside marriage it is fire in the bosom, and the man who takes it there will be burned. Many people believe they are the exception, strong enough or careful enough to handle temptation up close. The father’s question says that no one is.
27.notes: “Bosom” here is the same Hebrew word rendered “arms” in 5:20, “be embraced in the arms of a seductress.”

28.brief: A second question repeats the point: can anyone walk on hot coals without scorching his feet? Some things cannot be done safely, no matter how careful a person thinks he is.
28.explain:
“Can one walk on hot coals,”

A second question repeats the point with a new picture. To walk on hot coals is to step onto burning embers, deliberately and one step after another.

“And his feet not be seared?”

His feet will be scorched. The first question pictured fire held close; this one pictures fire walked on. Adultery is a path as well as an embrace, and every step on it burns. Together the two questions leave no room for the idea that some careful way of sinning will spare the sinner. Some things cannot be done safely, however careful a person thinks he is.

29.brief: So it is with the man who goes in to his neighbor’s wife; whoever touches her will not go unpunished. Adultery carries consequences as sure as fire’s burn, and no one who commits it remains innocent.
29.explain:
“So is he who goes in to his neighbor’s wife;”

The father applies his pictures. “Goes in to” is a modest way of describing sexual relations. “His neighbor’s wife” names the person whose marriage is betrayed. Adultery is never only a matter between two people. It breaks into a neighbor’s home and marriage and wounds a husband who trusted those around him.

“Whoever touches her shall not be innocent.”

“Touches” again speaks modestly of sexual contact. “Shall not be innocent” means he will not be held guiltless and will not go unpunished. As surely as fire burns, consequences follow. No one who commits adultery can claim afterward that he did nothing wrong or that the outcome came as a surprise.
29.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “shall not be innocent” can mean either to be free of guilt or to be free from punishment. The NKJV and KJV keep the first sense; the ESV, NASB and the 1984 NIV the second (“go unpunished”). On either reading the adulterer does not escape.

30.brief: To sharpen the warning, the father compares adultery with theft. People do not despise a thief who steals because he is starving, since his need is understood.
30.explain:
“People do not despise a thief”

To sharpen the warning, the father compares adultery with theft. To “despise” is to look down on someone with contempt. People do not usually treat a hungry thief with scorn, because they understand what drove him.

“If he steals to satisfy himself when he is starving.”

The thief’s motive is real hunger. He steals to satisfy himself because he has nothing to eat. People understand that need, even if they do not excuse the act. The comparison prepares for the contrast to come. The adulterer has no such need; he is not starving. And as the next verse shows, even the thief whose motive is understood pays dearly.
30.notes: In Hebrew “to satisfy himself” is literally ‘to fill his soul,’ where “soul” means his appetite and, more broadly, his life; the KJV keeps “his soul.” The same Hebrew word stands at the end of 6:32, where the adulterer “destroys his own soul.”

31.brief: Yet even that thief must pay back sevenfold when caught, perhaps giving up everything in his house. If theft driven by hunger still costs so much, adultery, which has no such excuse, will cost far more.
31.explain:
“Yet when he is found, he must restore sevenfold;”

“Yet” brings the turn. Even the hungry thief, once caught, must make restitution. “Sevenfold” uses the number seven to signal complete repayment. The line is best read as saying he must repay in full, whatever it costs him, rather than naming a precise legal penalty.

“He may have to give up all the substance of his house.”

Paying back may take everything he owns. The thief who stole because he had nothing may end with nothing. The argument moves from the lesser case to the greater. If a thief driven by hunger, whom people pity, still pays this much, then the adulterer, who has no such excuse and has taken something that can never be returned, will pay far more.
31.notes: In the cases set out in Exodus 22, the Law of Moses required double restitution in several situations (Exodus 22:4, 7, 9) and fourfold or fivefold for a sheep or an ox that had been slaughtered or sold (Exodus 22:1). None of these cases names a sevenfold payment, so “sevenfold” here is best taken as full repayment rather than a fixed legal penalty.

32.brief: Whoever commits adultery lacks understanding, and the man who does it destroys his own soul. Unlike the hungry thief, he gains nothing he needs; he wrecks himself.
32.explain:
“Whoever commits adultery with a woman lacks understanding;”

The father now states his verdict. The adulterer lacks understanding. He lacks sense, the inner judgment that sees where a path leads. Unlike the thief, he cannot plead hunger; he has acted against all good sense. The same Hebrew expression describes the young man “devoid of understanding” in 7:7, who walks toward the seductress’s house as evening falls.

“He who does so destroys his own soul.”

The adulterer destroys his own soul. His “soul” here means his whole self, his life. The thief stole to fill his own appetite, as 6:30 says; the adulterer ruins himself. Adultery promises satisfaction and delivers destruction. It wounds others, as 6:29 and 6:34 show, and the man who commits it also brings ruin on himself. He cannot blame anyone else for what he has done to himself.
32.notes: In Hebrew “lacks understanding” is literally “lacks heart,” as the KJV margin notes. In Proverbs the heart is the seat of thought and judgment, so a man who “lacks heart” lacks sense. Besides 7:7, the same Hebrew expression appears in 9:4, of those Wisdom calls.

33.brief: He will receive wounds and dishonor, and his reproach will not be wiped away. The shame among people lasts long after the act, though God still offers mercy to those who confess (28:13).
33.explain:
“Wounds and dishonor he will get,”

The consequences include wounds, physical blows or injury, and dishonor, public disgrace. In context the wounds may come from the wronged husband described in 6:34. The adulterer loses his standing among people as well as his peace.

“And his reproach will not be wiped away.”

“Reproach” is shame, the mark a man carries in the eyes of others. It will not be wiped away; the community remembers. The line describes lasting consequences among people. It does not set a limit on God’s mercy. God offers forgiveness to everyone who confesses and turns from sin: “whoever confesses and forsakes them will have mercy” (28:13). David found that mercy after his own adultery, when Nathan told him, “The LORD also has put away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13), yet the consequences in his household continued. Both truths stand together: forgiveness is real, and so are consequences that last.

34.brief: Jealousy is a husband’s fury, and he will not spare the adulterer in the day of vengeance. The wronged husband’s anger is fierce and unyielding.
34.explain:
“For jealousy is a husband’s fury;”

“For” explains why the adulterer’s wounds and dishonor are sure. The wronged husband’s jealousy turns to fury. Jealousy here is the protective, burning anger of a man whose marriage has been violated. The adulterer has wounded a real person, and that person will respond.

“Therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance.”

“The day of vengeance” is the time when the husband seeks to repay the wrong. “He will not spare” means he will show no mercy and hold nothing back. The fire the adulterer took into his bosom in 6:27 is now met by the fire of a husband’s anger. The Law of Moses, in Leviticus 20:10, treated adultery as a capital offense, but the proverb speaks of the husband’s personal response and does not say what form his vengeance would take.

35.brief: No payment will satisfy him, and many gifts will not appease him. Unlike the thief’s debt, this wrong cannot be bought off, which is why the father warns his son so strongly to stay away.
35.explain:
“He will accept no recompense,”

“Recompense” is compensation, a payment offered to settle a wrong; the Hebrew word can also mean a ransom, the price paid to free a life. The thief’s debt could be paid, even at great cost, as 6:31 showed, but this husband will accept no payment for what has been done to him.

“Nor will he be appeased though you give many gifts.”

No amount of gifts will calm his anger. Some wrongs cannot be bought off. The chapter that began with a son caught by a pledge for another person’s debt ends with a man facing a debt that no money can settle. That is why the father warns so strongly. The only safe course is the one he has just given: keep the commandment as a lamp, guard the heart and the eyes, and stay away from a fire that no one can carry without being burned.
35.notes: The NASB renders “recompense” as “ransom.” In Hebrew the line reads literally that he will not ‘lift the face’ of any ransom, which the KJV margin gives as ‘He will not accept the face of any ransom.’ The picture is of a man who will not even look with favor on the payment held out to him, which is why the KJV can say ‘He will not regard any ransom’ and the NKJV simply that he will accept no recompense.
